biographies.0: Mengde. A talented and ambitious leader with exceptional strategic vision. After fighting the Yellow Turbans and Dong Zhuo, he controlled the emperor to command the lords. Decades of war unified the north and laid the foundations of Wei.
biographies.1: Yuanrang. Cao Cao's kinsman and a leading Wei general. Cao Xing shot out his left eye during the campaign against Lu Bu; he pulled out the arrow, swallowed the eye and killed Cao Xing. Cao Cao trusted him deeply. Cao Pi later made him General-in-Chief.
biographies.3: Yunchang. Sworn brother of Liu Bei and Zhang Fei, devoted to restoring the Han. Famed for valor and loyalty, he slew Yan Liang and Wen Chou, traveled far to rejoin Liu Bei, and flooded seven armies. He headed Shu's Five Tiger Generals.
biographies.5: Zixiao. Cao Cao's kinsman, who served from his first campaigns. He inspired troops in desperate situations and often turned defeat into victory. Chen Jiao praised his godlike courage. He later became Wei's Grand Marshal.
biographies.6: Miaocai. He married Cao Cao's daughter. A bold Wei general famed for swift surprise attacks. While defending Mount Dingjun, he fell into Fa Zheng's trap and was slain by Huang Zhong.
biographies.10: Wenqian. Originally a civil officer, he became one of Cao Cao's five great generals. With Zhang Liao and Li Dian, he defended Hefei against Eastern Wu and earned great distinction.
biographies.11: Mancheng. A Wei general who served Cao Cao from the Yellow Turban campaigns. Calm and cautious through many battles, he often restrained reckless colleagues. He defended Hefei alongside Zhang Liao and Yue Jin.
biographies.12: Zilian. Cao Cao's cousin, who joined him with Cao Ren. A core commander of Cao's army, he fought across the realm and saved Cao Cao from danger several times.
biographies.32: Xuande. Descendant of Liu Sheng, Prince Jing of Zhongshan. Cao Cao regarded him as a hero of the age. He gathered gifted followers and founded Shu. After Emperor Xian abdicated, he proclaimed himself emperor of Shu Han.
biographies.33: Yide. Sworn brother of Liu Bei and Guan Yu, fighting to restore the Han. He held off Cao Cao's army alone at Changban and won repeated victories in Sichuan. A General of Chariots and Cavalry and one of Shu's Five Tiger Generals.
biographies.91: Gongfu. A veteran who served three generations of the Sun family, beginning with Sun Jian. At Red Cliffs he accepted punishment to make a false surrender convincing, enabling Wu's fire attack to rout Cao Cao and winning lasting fame.
biographies.98: Demou. A veteran of three generations of the Sun family, wielding an iron-ridged serpent spear. At Red Cliffs he served as deputy commander under Zhou Yu and helped defeat Cao Cao's army.
biographies.99: Wentai. Descendant of the strategist Sun Tzu. As governor of Changsha he led the coalition vanguard against Dong Zhuo. First into Luoyang, he found the Imperial Seal. He later died in an ambush while attacking Liu Biao.
biographies.101: Benchu. Head of the prestigious Yuan family and elected leader of the coalition against Dong Zhuo. He later challenged Cao Cao for the Central Plains. Indecision and rejection of loyal counsel led to division and defeat at Guandu.
biographies.119: Fengxian. Celebrated alongside his horse Red Hare for unmatched martial skill, archery and horsemanship. Fickle in loyalty, he repeatedly betrayed his masters. Betrayed by his own men, he was captured by Cao Cao, strangled and beheaded.
biographies.127: Governor of Xiliang. During the struggle between He Jin and the eunuchs, he entered Luoyang and seized power. He deposed the young emperor and installed Emperor Xian. His tyranny threw the realm into chaos and ushered in the Three Kingdoms era.
biographies.128: Dong Zhuo's General of Chariots and Cavalry and Zhang Xiu's uncle. His wife, Lady Zou, was renowned for her beauty. Short of supplies, he attacked Liu Biao at Nanyang and was killed by an arrow.
biographies.129: An officer of Dong Zhuo. After Dong Zhuo's death, Jia Xu advised him to attack Chang'an. He killed Wang Yun and shared control of the court with Li Jue. Later reduced to banditry, he was killed by his subordinate Wu Xi.
biographies.130: An officer of Dong Zhuo. He pursued Cao Cao after Lu Bu's ambush and shot him in the shoulder, but was slain by Xiahou Dun when the latter rode to the rescue.
biographies.131: A favored officer of Dong Zhuo. With Guo Si, he retook Chang'an in the name of revenge, killed Wang Yun, seized Emperor Xian and expelled Lu Bu. His tyranny continued until Yang Biao's scheme turned him against Guo Si.
biographies.132: Dong Zhuo's son-in-law and strategist. His plans helped Dong Zhuo seize power, recruit Lu Bu and defeat the lords. He saw through Wang Yun's linked stratagem but his warnings were ignored. He was executed after Dong Zhuo's death.
biographies.133: An officer of Dong Zhuo. After his lord's death, he defeated Ma Teng and Han Sui. Remembering their shared hometown, he let Han Sui escape during the pursuit. Li Jue and Guo Si had him killed for it.
biographies.134: A towering warrior serving Dong Zhuo. He volunteered to face the coalition, defeated Sun Jian and slew Bao Zhong, Zu Mao, Yu She and Pan Feng. Guan Yu later killed him with a single stroke.
biographies.135: An officer of Dong Zhuo. He gave Red Hare to Lu Bu and persuaded him to defect to Dong Zhuo. Later he joined Wang Yun's assassination plot, posing as an imperial envoy to lure Dong Zhuo into the palace.
biographies.145: Governor of Xuzhou and a coalition lord against Dong Zhuo. When Cao Cao invaded to avenge his father, the elderly, ailing Tao Qian repeatedly offered Xuzhou to Liu Bei, who had come to his aid.
biographies.146: Zhang Jiao's younger brother and a leader of the Yellow Turban Rebellion. Calling himself General of the Earth, he commanded rebels with sorcery learned from his brother. He was later assassinated by his subordinate Yan Zheng.
biographies.147: Younger brother of Zhang Jiao and Zhang Bao. A Yellow Turban leader calling himself General of Humanity. He continued commanding the rebels after Zhang Jiao's death, but was defeated by imperial troops and died at Quyang.

class_descriptions: Ruler class I. A balanced, versatile unit effective in both attacks and tactics.
Ruler class II. A wider attack range makes this versatile unit even more useful.
Ruler class III. Improved movement completes a well-rounded unit.
Infantry I. Excellent defense and strong attacks against archers, but ordinary offense against cavalry.
Infantry II. Strong defense makes a reliable wall for the army. Also resists tactics well.
Infantry III. Improved movement and strong defense make a dependable frontline unit.
Archer I. Ranged attacks are highly effective against cavalry, but infantry poses a serious threat.
Archer II. Greater range improves flexibility; lethal shots can decide a battle.
Archer III. Elite marksmen with exceptional range.
Cavalry I. Excellent movement and attack; resists infantry, but is vulnerable to bows and catapults.
Cavalry II. Fast movement enables powerful charges. Beware of advancing without support.
Cavalry III. Even greater movement; use it to break through enemy lines.
Mounted archer I. A mobile ranged unit with powerful attacks against cavalry.
Mounted archer II. Shorter range than foot archers, but greater attack power.
Mounted archer III. Improved range and movement; works well alongside cavalry.
Catapult I. Exceptional range. Training turns it into a powerful weapon.
Catapult II. Attacks cover a wider area, damaging more enemies.
Catapult III. Improved movement and range provide decisive ranged support.
Martial artist I. High agility favors evasion and double attacks. Can also use tactics.
Martial artist II. Wider attack range and agile movement make it flexible.
Martial artist III. A master of martial arts with improved movement.
Bandit I. High attack and morale; excels in mountains and wasteland, with frequent critical hits.
Bandit II. Can use earth tactics. Lure enemies onto favorable terrain.
Bandit III. Improved movement and frequent critical hits overwhelm opponents.
Strategist I. A civil unit specializing in offensive fire, water and earth tactics.
Strategist II. Stronger offensive tactics are especially effective against enemies with low Spirit.
Strategist III. Devastating tactical power, but vulnerable to attacks from behind.
Healer I. Uses recovery tactics. Essential support behind the battle line.
Healer II. Improved movement lets it support more friendly units.
Healer III. Further improved movement makes it a reliable rescue unit.
Taoist I. Uses disruptive tactics to weaken enemy fighting power.
Taoist II. Many tactics ignore weather and terrain, making it convenient to use.
Taoist III. Improved movement and deceptive tactics undermine the enemy's state of mind.
Mounted strategist I. Offensive tactics with movement equal to cavalry.
Mounted strategist II. Specializes in fire and wind. Only this class can alter weather.
Mounted strategist III. Greater speed makes excellent support for mounted troops.
Dancer I. Similar abilities to a martial artist. Can cure nearby allies' status ailments.
Dancer II. Wide attack range and a small but useful selection of tactics.
Dancer III. Improved movement and agility allow freedom across the battlefield.
Outstanding attack and defense make this among the strongest martial units. Weak against tactics.
Followers of the Way of Peace who rose in armed rebellion. Named for their yellow headscarves.
A powerful unit on water terrain. Avoid fighting where the enemy has the terrain advantage.
Commands bears with powerful attacks that may immobilize foes. Weak against bows and tactics.
Commands agile tigers. A charge can trigger counters from two foes. Weak against bows and tactics.
A civil unit strong on water terrain. Its high attack punishes anyone who underestimates it.
Uses offensive, disruptive and recovery tactics. Among the strongest civil units; beware.
Can use all tactics. Detached from worldly affairs, it has little battle experience.
Transports supplies. Cannot attack.
Transports food. Cannot attack.
A wooden puppet whose attacks poison enemies. Apparently weak against tactics; details are unknown.
A clay puppet whose attacks confuse enemies. Apparently weak against tactics; details are unknown.
The Han emperor. Cannot attack.
Innocent civilians with no combat training. Cannot attack.
item_descriptions: A small sword. Initially modest, it grows stronger with training.
A long, heavy sword, stronger than a short sword.
The most powerful standard sword.
A short spear. Its power grows with training.
A long, heavy spear, stronger than a short spear.
The most powerful standard spear.
A small bow. Its power grows with training.
A large, heavy bow, stronger than a short bow.
An iron bow, the strongest standard bow.
A wooden staff. Its power grows with training.
A bronze staff, stronger than a wooden staff.
An iron staff, the strongest standard staff.
A wooden catapult. Its power grows with training.
A bronze catapult, stronger than the wooden version.
An iron catapult, the strongest standard catapult.
A bamboo fan. Its power grows with training.
A military fan, stronger than a bamboo fan.
An iron fan, the strongest standard fan.
A stone ritual sword. Its power grows with training.
A bronze ritual sword, stronger than the stone version.
An iron ritual sword, the strongest standard ritual sword.
Liu Bei's paired swords, forged after the Peach Garden oath. They allow a counterattack after an enemy's counter.
Cao Cao's sword carried by Xiahou En, taken by Zhao Yun at Changban in the novel. Especially effective against cavalry; also called the Horse-Cutting Sword.
Cao Cao's sword, paired with Qinggang. Its broad, sturdy blade can serve as a shield against attacks.
Sun Jian's prized blade. Light and easy to wield, it makes its user more agile.
Guan Yu's great blade, weighing eighty-two jin. Its power prevents enemy counterattacks.
Zhang Fei's spear, with a snake-shaped tip. A forceful thrust can pierce two units.
Lu Bu's halberd, with a crescent blade beside its point. Its bloodthirsty power can trigger another attack after a killing blow.
Lu Bu's powerful bow. Its arrows can prevent enemies from moving.
The bow of Han's Flying General Li Guang. Also called the Demon-Breaking Bow, it can seal enemy tactics.
Metal weights linked by an iron chain. Its unpredictable strikes can confuse enemies.
A pair of whips. Allows a counterattack after an enemy's counter.
A cannon firing scorching liquid-metal shells. Its attacks can poison enemies.
A divine fan that raises great winds, wielded by Princess Iron Fan in Journey to the West. Strengthens wind tactics.
A divine fan that raises fierce flames, wielded by Yang Ren in Investiture of the Gods. Strengthens fire tactics.
Zhuge Liang's white-feather fan. Its spiritual power reduces the MP cost of tactics.
Wang Yun's sword, borrowed by Cao Cao for his attempt on Dong Zhuo. Improves tactic success rates.
A sage's sword that grants spiritual power and increases maximum MP.
Leather armor. Its protection improves with training.
Bronze armor, stronger than leather armor.
Iron armor, the strongest standard armor.
Cloth clothing. Its protection improves with training.
Leather clothing, stronger than a cloth robe.
Battle clothing with the best standard robe defense.
Armor set with dazzling mirrors that block indirect attacks from bows and catapults.
Golden armor that protects its wearer against critical hits.
Flexible chain armor that prevents double attacks.
Silver armor that resists tactics and reduces their damage.
Dragon-scale armor. Uses MP in place of HP damage from normal attacks.
Clothing embroidered with flying dragons. Made for close combat and improved agility.
Zhuge Liang's customary cloak. Increases the wearer's Spirit.
Black cloth imbued with spiritual power. Increases maximum MP.
A robe woven from phoenix feathers. Its power continually restores the wearer's HP.
A leather shield that improves evasion of enemy attacks.
A bronze shield, more effective than leather.
A silver shield that improves evasion of enemy tactics.
The Wind God's shield. Improves defense against both attacks and tactics.
Leather horse armor for cavalry. Reduces ranged damage to offset cavalry's weakness against it.
Bronze horse armor, more effective than leather barding.
Light, strong wheels usable only by catapults. Increase movement.
Cao Cao's famous horse. Increases movement.
Cao Cao's famous horse. Increases movement.
Lu Bu's famed horse, given by Dong Zhuo to win his loyalty. Allows unrestricted charge movement.
Liu Bei's famous horse, known for leaping the Tan River. Passable terrain costs only one movement point.
A leather helm that raises maximum HP. Helms are for infantry classes.
A bronze helm, more effective than leather.
An iron helm, the strongest helm. Greatly raises maximum HP.
A cap favored by recluses. Raises maximum MP.
A scholar's cap, more effective than the square cap.
Zhuge Liang's favored cap. The strongest cap, greatly raising maximum MP.
Cloth gloves prevent slipping and improve attack accuracy.
Leather gloves, more effective than cloth.
A sharp throwing stone, called a featherless arrow. Allows ranged attacks; usable only by bandit classes.
Sun Wu's military treatise from the Spring and Autumn era. Grants EXP each turn.
Cao Cao's military treatise. Increases EXP gained.
Physician Hua Tuo's medical book. Restores HP each turn.
A medical book found in the mountains by Yu Ji. Cures poison, confusion, immobilization and silence each turn.
A book of arts given to Zhang Jiao by the Immortal of the Southern Lands. Restores MP each turn.
A book of arts found by Zuo Ci on Mount Emei. Allows imitation of adjacent units' tactics.
Taigong Wang's military treatise. Grants weapon EXP each turn.
A military treatise famed alongside Six Teachings. Grants armor EXP each turn.
A bag of healing beans. Automatically uses a bean when attacks or tactics reduce the unit's HP.
The Imperial Seal, said to grant its owner the realm. Its special power is said to make every attack critical.
An azure orb used to summon the Azure Dragon. Only mounted strategists can equip it.
A red orb used to summon the Vermilion Bird. Only strategists can equip it.
A black orb used to summon the Black Tortoise. Only Taoists can equip it.
A white orb used to summon the White Tiger. Only healers can equip it.
Magic beans that restore HP. Modest effect, but inexpensive.
Magic rice that restores a substantial amount of HP.
A rare magic peach that fully restores HP.
Expensive magic water that restores MP.
Potent medicinal wine that restores MP.
Medicine made from detoxifying herbs. Cures poison.
A very bitter medicine that cures confusion.
A plaster applied to the feet to cure immobilization.
A pleasant medicine that cures silence.
Medicine that cures poison, confusion, immobilization and silence.
Required for class promotion. At a sufficient level, promotes the unit and fully restores HP and MP.
A magic fruit that raises Strength and slightly improves Attack.
A magic fruit that raises Intellect and slightly improves Spirit.
A magic fruit that raises Leadership and slightly improves Defense.
A magic fruit that improves quickness and slightly raises Agility.
A magic fruit that raises Luck and slightly improves Morale.
A magic fruit that increases EXP or level, and fully restores HP and MP.
